video_title: Why the Next Great Founders Will Be Borderless
gist: a16z investors Angela Strange and Gabriel Vasquez lay out the firm's 'borderless founder' thesis: AI is simultaneously democratizing startup-building everywhere and concentrating the fastest-moving activity in the Bay Area, so a16z built diaspora communities, local-luminary networks, and onboarding infrastructure (visas, hacker houses) to capture international founders who bring differentiated talent, home-country brand, and enterprise-customer access.

themes.theme: Origins: From Canada's C100 to LatAm's WhatsApp Diaspora

insights.claim: Angela Strange's international investing thesis began when her brother, who had joined Nubank in Brazil, relayed the idea that emerging markets offer 'five fat, happy banks that only serve 20% of the population' versus the brutal competition of trying to become the fifth financial-services option for an already-served US consumer.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: A reusable market-entry heuristic: underbanked, under-served markets with high friction (licensing, infrastructure build-out) can beat saturated developed markets despite higher initial cost.
insights.quote: you could compete to be the fifth financial services for every customer in the US. Or you could go to a wide open market with five fat, happy banks that only serve 20% of the population.

insights.claim: a16z's first Latin America check went to Addi's CEO Santiago Suárez, and the Colombian fintech now serves roughly a quarter of Colombia's population for banking and payments.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: Illustrates achievable market-share concentration for early movers in underbanked fintech markets — a benchmark for evaluating other LatAm fintech penetration claims.
insights.quote: now serves a quarter of the Colombian population for banking and payments.

insights.claim: Gabriel Vasquez independently mapped the Latin American founder landscape early in his a16z tenure and found only about 30 unicorns existed in the entire region at the time, small enough that he could personally connect the 25 most important CEOs into a single WhatsApp group.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Early-stage regional ecosystems can be small enough for one well-connected investor to map and access nearly the whole founder base directly — a structural edge for first movers into a new geography.
insights.quote: there were only 30 unicorns in Latin America.

insights.claim: a16z's diaspora-network model has a roughly 15-year precedent in C100, a group of about 100 Canadians in the Bay Area that Angela Strange helped found to give Canadian startups design partners and executives; that Canadian diaspora has since produced unicorns including Shopify and OpenEvidence.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: A ~15-year track record showing diaspora-alumni networks reliably produce unicorn-scale outcomes — the template a16z is now replicating for other countries under the borderless-founder banner.

insights.claim: AI is structurally different from earlier tech waves for globalization: it democratizes the ability to build startups anywhere in the world, but simultaneously concentrates the fastest-moving activity in the Bay Area more than before, reversing a16z's earlier model of flying to founders in favor of founders converging on Silicon Valley.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'AI decentralizes innovation everywhere' narrative — hub advantage may be self-reinforcing even as building tools diffuse globally, which matters for where seed-stage AI dealflow physically clusters.
insights.quote: this technology is very democratic. It distributes the ability to get it anywhere in the world. It opens up other markets, but then it also concentrates the kind of epicenter of where things are moving the fastest to the Bay Area.

insights.claim: After the AI wave hit, demand from Brazilian and Colombian founders shifted from wanting a16z's team to fly down and connect locally to wanting to be brought into and integrated with the Bay Area directly.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Signals strengthening capital and talent gravity toward Silicon Valley in the AI era, relevant to where AI-native founder sourcing should concentrate resources.

insights.claim: a16z deliberately defines 'borderless founder' broadly as anyone building with global ambitions rather than narrowly as 'immigrant founder,' since even domestic founders from overlooked places (a small German town, rural US areas) carry the same drive to prove themselves globally.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Reframes founder-sourcing criteria beyond geography or visa status toward psychology and ambition — a screen for identifying outlier founders regardless of home base.
insights.quote: anyone international, whether you're building primarily in your home country to start, but that you have global ambitions, you're a borderless founder.

insights.claim: a16z's 'borderless dinners,' originally small (20-30 person) Latin-America-only gatherings hosted for visiting founders with help from figures like Brex co-founder Pedro Franceschi, have matured to the point where early attendees have themselves become unicorn founders now speaking to the next cohort.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: A compounding community flywheel is emerging — informal event infrastructure turning into a self-sustaining alumni network, a durable moat versus capital-only competitors.

insights.claim: Addi's rapid rise in Colombia let it recruit a credit officer capable of underwriting billions in GMV away from Capital One in Virginia, not by outbidding on pay but by becoming 'the hottest company in Colombia' versus one of 50 look-alike fintechs in the US.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: Brand concentration in a smaller market can out-recruit larger, better-funded but undifferentiated US competitors for scarce specialist talent.
insights.quote: you become the hottest company in Colombia

insights.claim: Taco, an a16z-backed payroll/HR company targeting Brazilian bureaucracy, was able to recruit Brazilian talent back from the US because those recruits understood the local bureaucratic problems firsthand and believed the right AI and team could finally fix them.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: A repatriation-driven talent flow is emerging as its own sourcing and hiring channel for companies tackling deep local-market problems.

insights.claim: ElevenLabs, founded by Polish founders and based in the UK, became a source of national pride in Poland — likened to an 'AI Olympics' where each country wants its own flagship winner — and received direct investment from the Polish government.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: National-pride-driven government backing can function as a distribution and validation subsidy for portfolio companies — a soft-power tailwind worth watching in company selection.
insights.quote: the Polish government just invested in 11 Labs and is going to do a bunch of initiatives with them.

insights.claim: Similar to Poland and ElevenLabs, the Swedish government has publicly backed Lovable, and that state validation gives portfolio companies a credibility stamp that accelerates enterprise sales even in markets outside the home country.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Government sponsorship is becoming a repeatable enterprise-sales unlock for AI-native national champions, not a one-off case.

insights.claim: Jeeves works with Brazil's central bank to move corporate money internationally via stablecoins, and that regulatory relationship is building its reputation as the most trusted, fast, compliant option for enterprises, which in turn compounds into easier talent attraction.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: Deep regulatory relationships, not just product, are becoming a defensible moat in cross-border payments/stablecoin infrastructure — worth tracking as a differentiator in that competitive set.

insights.claim: Factor Labs' early design partnership with the conglomerate owned by the Slim family, the largest business group in Latin America, expanded into additional workflows within that same corporation over time.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Landing one dominant conglomerate in a concentrated market can function as a multi-year account-expansion engine — a repeatable pattern for enterprise-software bets in LatAm.

insights.claim: Supersonic, founded in Spain, landed Salesforce as a design partner and eventually a paying customer after its founder connected with a fellow university alumnus who was Salesforce's former CRO and later became its COO.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Alumni-network-driven enterprise sales can compress the traditional cold-outreach cycle for early-stage cross-border startups.

insights.claim: Cognition, a prominent Silicon Valley AI coding company, generated an outsized share of its early revenue from Brazil because enterprises there wanted to adopt AI quickly but had few local providers to choose from, showing the borderless bridge also runs from the US outward.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: US-born AI startups can find outsized, underserved early revenue in emerging markets hungry to adopt AI where local supply is thin — a go-to-market lever many SV-only startups ignore.

themes.theme: Ecosystem-Building Playbook: Luminaries, Scouts, Repeat Founders

insights.claim: a16z's method for entering a new geography centers on finding 'local luminaries' — highly respected local founders or angels regardless of their own company's ultimate scale; in Sweden, the founders of a Lime-like scooter company turned out to be central angel-investing hubs behind much of the country's AI boom.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: When scoping a new geography, investors should map 'local luminaries' — who need not have had outsized company outcomes themselves — as a proxy for network density before deploying capital.
insights.quote: you wouldn't have thought that they will be in the middle of of the AI boom in Sweden

insights.claim: Gabriel Peterson, a Swedish high-school dropout who moved to the US with no formal education, worked at Midjourney, became one of the youngest researchers at OpenAI, and later started his own company, now serves as the default connector for other Swedish founders relocating to Silicon Valley.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: A single credentialed 'rising star' can become critical relationship infrastructure for an entire national founder cohort — a leading indicator that a country's ecosystem is about to inflect.
insights.quote: high school dropout from Sweden, came to the US with no education, got a job at Mid Journey, then became one of the youngest researchers at OpenAI and now he started a company.

insights.claim: a16z runs a global scout program that recruits rising executives (heads of sales, founding engineers with some liquidity) out of its portfolio companies specifically because they are mission-driven to pay forward what they learned to the next generation of founders in their home ecosystems.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: Portfolio-company alumni-as-scouts is a scalable, low-headcount way to extend sourcing reach into new geographies.

insights.claim: a16z specifically targets repeat founders from emerging markets who reached a $1-5B outcome in an earlier, harder cycle but didn't fully realize their vision; reconnecting them with Stanford-caliber engineering talent and customer conversations won a16z the deal on a new company (pip.com) even against investors who already had pre-existing relationships with the founder.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: A cohort of 'graduated' emerging-market founders with prior $1-5B outcomes is an identifiable, underserved sourcing pool for the next venture cycle of larger cross-border companies.
insights.quote: this this $5 billion exit or $5 billion outcome wasn't enough for me. I want to do something greater from my local ecosystem.

themes.theme: Onboarding Infrastructure: Visas, Hacker Houses, Timing

insights.claim: a16z is an investor in Extraordinary, a visa-focused company that helps international founders determine the right US visa category and secure qualifying recommendation letters, framed as one of the single most stressful parts of relocating to Silicon Valley.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Immigration-services infrastructure is becoming an investable adjacency to the founder-mobility thesis, not just a support service.
insights.quote: it's the the most stressful process when it when it comes to moving to to the US is like what is the right visa?

insights.claim: a16z sponsored Palo House, a hacker house in Palo Alto founded by four students from Germany's CDTM program who met the firm at the Slush conference in Finland; over four months it hosted roughly 1,200 visitors, becoming an informal channel a16z uses to route incoming international founders into its borderless-dinner network.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Physical co-living infrastructure in the Bay Area is a measurable, replicable channel for early-stage international deal sourcing.
insights.quote: it was like 1,200 people that end up staying there.

insights.claim: a16z's standing advice to prospective international founders is to spend at least 3-6 months physically in Silicon Valley before deciding whether to relocate, since trips of only a few weeks are rarely long enough to penetrate the network and calibrate to the region's operating speed.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable benchmark international founders — and investors scouting them — can use to judge the seriousness of a relocation decision.
insights.quote: at the very least 3 to 6 months to you can kind of emerge

themes.theme: Macro Outlook: Two-Country Companies and Shifting Return Concentration

insights.claim: Roughly 40% of a16z's investments are now in international founders, split about evenly between those based in the US and those based abroad, according to internal stats the firm ran.
insights.speaker: Angela Strange
insights.so_what: A concrete portfolio-level KPI showing how far a top-tier US VC firm's capital has already shifted toward non-domestic founders — a proxy for where future outlier outcomes may originate.
insights.quote: 40% of our investments were in international founders you know half of them were based here half of them were based in other countries

insights.claim: Against the long-cited claim that roughly 90% of venture returns come from Silicon Valley-based companies, Gabriel Vasquez wants that non-SV share to grow from about 10% to 20-30%, arguing the current framing undercounts 'borderless' companies effectively claimed by two countries (US headquarters, engineering team based abroad).
insights.speaker: Gabriel Vasquez
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'where do venture returns come from' question for LPs and allocators — the honest attribution for many top outcomes may increasingly be dual-country rather than single-geography.
insights.quote: if if that share goes from 10% all the way to 20 to 30% that's something that I would like to see
